analysis.one_liner: Bans patents on human genes and naturally occurring genetic sequences.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed patent law to bar anyone from getting a patent on a human nucleotide sequence, its functions or correlations, or the naturally occurring products it specifies [S2, S3]. At the time, companies held patents on human genes, which meant they could charge monopoly prices for genetic tests and control who could study or use a gene [S2]. The bill applied only going forward, so patents already issued would have stayed in force [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients needing genetic tests (like tests for breast cancer risk), who would face more competition and potentially lower prices once genes could not be exclusively patented; researchers and laboratories, who could study and test on any human gene sequence without negotiating licenses; and doctors, who could use genetic information without infringement risk [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, researchers, and genetic testing labs

how_it_helps.text: No new patents could be obtained on a nucleotide sequence, its functions or correlations, or the naturally occurring products it specifies, ending exclusive claims over parts of the human genome [S2, S3].
The bill would have kept anyone from using patent law to block genetic research or to hold a monopoly over a diagnostic test built on a naturally occurring human gene [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies holding or seeking gene patents — genetic testing firms and biotech investors — would lose the ability to claim exclusive rights over human gene sequences and to collect licensing fees and monopoly prices on gene-based tests [S2, S3]. Biotech firms also argued, in general, that patents are what attract investment into gene-based research and diagnostics.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: patents are a main incentive for biotech investment, so a blanket ban on gene patents could have reduced funding for genetic research and test development — the counterargument the bill's supporters would have had to answer.
The ban covered not just sequences but their 'functions or correlations,' broad language that could have created legal uncertainty over how far the prohibition reached [S3].
The bill did nothing about patents already issued; existing gene monopolies would have remained in force until they expired [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people, the upside was clear: no more exclusive patents on naturally occurring human genes, meaning cheaper genetic tests and freer research. The downside was the credible concern that removing gene patents could dampen investment in developing genetic tests in the first place. In the end the question was settled partly by others: the Supreme Court's 2013 Myriad decision later invalidated patents on isolated naturally occurring DNA, reaching a similar result through the courts rather than Congress — a widely known development outside these sources.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its intellectual property subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Xavier Becerra introduced the bill on February 9, 2007, joined by Rep. Dave Weldon, a Florida Republican, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S3, S5].
On March 1, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property — a subcommittee that handles patent bills — where it stayed [S5].
No further action of any kind appears in the record through the end of the 110th Congress in January 2009: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
The bill carried bipartisan sponsorship — six cosponsors, five Democrats and one Republican — but that support never translated into committee action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Holders of existing human gene patents — genetic testing companies and biotech investors with exclusive rights over gene sequences — were better off, because no competing bill moved and their monopolies continued. Patients paying monopoly prices for gene-based tests and researchers needing licenses kept bearing those costs, though the Supreme Court's 2013 Myriad ruling later removed patent protection for isolated natural DNA through a different route.

for.name: Xavier Becerra
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban patents on human genetic material and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Dave Weldon
for.what_they_did: Joined Becerra as the bill's Republican co-lead at introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. John Conyers Jr. (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after receiving the referral; the record shows no committee action beyond sending it to a subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship itself was bipartisan — a Democratic lead sponsor, a Republican co-lead, and six cosponsors split five Democrats to one Republican — but no vote was ever recorded, so the bill's fate was decided by committee inaction rather than a party-split roll call [S3, S4, S5].

industries.industry: Gene-patent holders and genetic testing companies
industries.note: These companies claimed exclusive patents on human gene sequences and charged monopoly prices for tests and licenses; the bill would have ended new patents of that kind, cutting their exclusive revenue. Their interest in keeping the patents ran directly against patients' interest in affordable genetic testing.

Gene patents attract investment into diagnostics and therapies, so a ban could have reduced funding for gene-based research; the bill's backers argued that natural gene monopolies instead raised costs and blocked research. Gains and losses for this group genuinely cut both ways.
